title: Systems with Infinitely Many Solutions Core Test
description: Practice and explain systems with infinitely many solutions.

questions.questionText: The equations y = 2x + 2 and 2y = 4x + 4 describe which graphs?
questions.correctAnswer: The same line
questions.explanation: Dividing the second equation by 2 gives the first equation, so every point on the line is shared.

questions.questionText: Subtracting equivalent equations 2x + y = 8 and 2x + y = 8 gives 0 = 0. What does this mean?
questions.correctAnswer: Infinitely many shared ordered pairs
questions.explanation: The identity shows that the two equations impose the same condition, not that both coordinates must be zero.

questions.questionText: Complete a copy of x + y = 7: 3x + 3y = __.
questions.explanation: Multiplying an equation by 3 requires multiplying both sides, including the constant, by 3.

questions.questionText: Both equations of a system reduce to y = x + 2. Must (0, 0) solve the system?
questions.correctAnswer: No; the line does not pass through (0, 0).
questions.explanation: At x = 0 the shared line has y = 2, not zero. Infinite solutions are restricted to the shared line.
options: Yes; infinitely many solutions includes every point.
Yes; all lines pass through the origin.
No; the system has no solutions.
No; the line does not pass through (0, 0).

questions.questionText: A system has two copies of y = 2x. Which describes its solution set?
questions.correctAnswer: All pairs (t, 2t) for real t
questions.explanation: Choose any real x-value t; y must still equal the slope times t.

questions.questionText: For infinitely many solutions, what must k be in 2x + 3y = 8 and 6x + 9y = k?
questions.explanation: The coefficients are tripled, so the right side must be tripled too.

questions.questionText: Compare 2y = 4x + 6 with y = 2x + 4. Why are there not infinitely many solutions?
questions.correctAnswer: Their slopes match but their intercepts differ.
questions.explanation: The first equation is y = 2x + 3; the second has intercept 4. They are distinct parallel lines.
options: Multiplying by 2 changes the solution set.
Their slopes match but their intercepts differ.
The two equations describe the same line.

questions.questionText: The system is x + y = 12 and 4x + 4y = 48. Which listed pair is a solution?
questions.explanation: The pair sums to 12; multiplying that sum by 4 satisfies the second equation as well.

questions.questionText: A student doubles x + 2y = 7 and writes 2x + 4y = 7. What is the error?
questions.correctAnswer: The constant must also be doubled to 14.
questions.explanation: Equivalent equations require applying the nonzero multiplier to every term on both sides.
options: The constant must also be doubled to 14.

questions.questionText: After simplifying 2(x + y) + 2 = 14 and 3x + 3y = 18, a student says any pair is a solution. Which correction is complete?
questions.correctAnswer: There are infinitely many solutions, but only pairs with x + y = 6.
questions.explanation: The equations both reduce to x + y = 6. An identity after elimination leaves this original constraint in force.
options: There are no solutions because the constants differ.
There are infinitely many solutions, but only pairs with x + y = 6.

questions.questionText: For which (a, b) does the system 2x + 2y = 8 and ax + 6y = b have infinitely many solutions?
questions.explanation: The y coefficient forces a scale factor of 3. Both the x coefficient and constant must use that factor.

questions.questionText: The system x + y = 12, 2x + 2y = 24 has infinitely many real solutions. If x and y count objects and must be nonnegative integers, how many pairs are possible?
questions.explanation: Choose x from 0 through 12, inclusive; each gives one y. Context restricts the infinite real line to 13 pairs.

questions.questionText: A learner tests x = 0 in y = 2x + 5 and y = 3x + 5. Both give y = 5. Does this prove infinitely many solutions?
questions.correctAnswer: No; their different slopes mean they share only (0, 5).
questions.explanation: A shared point alone is insufficient. Subtracting the two expressions gives x = 0, so the only shared point is (0, 5).
options: Yes; one matching point proves equivalent equations.
No; their different slopes mean they share only (0, 5).
No; the system has no solutions.
Yes; equal intercepts always imply equal lines.

questions.questionText: Two real variables satisfy y = 2x + 2. A second rule is y - 2 = 2x. Which additional rule would select exactly one of the existing solutions?
questions.explanation: The original rules describe one line. Fixing x = 3 fixes y = 8; the other choices merely repeat the line.
